title: The Equation That Looks Ahead
outcome: Compute a finite-horizon optimal policy and its value by backward induction.
prerequisites: The mapped chapter and its notation

input_fields.states: Object mapping states to optional terminal:number and actions:list. Action has name,reward:number,probabilities:normalized list,next_states:aligned registered state keys.

equations.label: EQV7-01
explanations: Equation (7.1) collapses a whole future of rewards into one number, weighting later rewards less than earlier ones.
Add up every future reward, multiplying each by the discount factor raised to the number of steps away it is.

equations.label: EQV7-02
explanations: Equation (7.2) attaches a single number to a state, saying what the agent can expect to collect from there onward under a given way of behaving.
Average the return over everything that could happen from this state, under the policy the agent is following.

equations.label: EQV7-03
explanations: Equation (7.3) expresses a state's value in terms of the values of the states it leads to, turning a question about an infinite future into a relationship between neighbours.
Average over the actions the policy might take and the states each might lead to, taking the immediate reward plus the discounted value of where the agent arrives.

equations.label: EQV7-04
explanations: Equation (7.4) characterizes the best achievable value from every state, and the policy that achieves it falls out of the same expression.
For each action, average the immediate reward plus discounted next-state value over where it might lead, then keep the largest.

equations.label: chapter-07-display-5
explanations: Equation (7.5) turns a Bellman residual into an upper bound on value error for declared discounted model.
Divide largest one-step inconsistency by remaining contraction margin $1-\gamma$.
